topic: Day 1 · DKA Management III — Potassium & Electrolytes
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Diabetes & Acute Medicine Unit
speakerBio: Diabetologist and acute-medicine lead who chairs the trust's DKA governance group and has a standing rule that no trainee starts an insulin infusion until they have said the potassium number out loud.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes arrives in DKA: pH 7.05, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, glucose 31 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L. The house officer, delighted that the gas is finally back, hangs a litre of saline with a fixed-rate insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h and turns to the next patient. What nobody has looked at is the potassium: it reads 3.2 mmol/L. Ninety minutes later the monitor alarms — the T waves have flattened, U waves have appeared, and the rhythm degenerates into a broad-complex arrest. The insulin did exactly what insulin does: it drove potassium into cells. In a patient who was already total-body depleted, that was the last of the reserve. This session is about the electrolyte that quietly kills more DKA patients than the acidosis ever does — potassium — and the JBDS rule that would have saved this patient.

1 · 🧠 The potassium paradox — why the number lies

The single most dangerous misconception in DKA is that a normal or high serum potassium means the patient has enough potassium. It does not. In DKA, the patient is always total-body potassium depleted — typically by 3–5 mmol/kg, or 200–400 mmol in an adult — even when the serum reading is high on arrival. The serum number and the total-body store are telling you two completely different stories.

The mechanism, drawn out step by step

  1. Insulin deficiency removes the main stimulus that normally pushes K⁺ into cells via the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump. Potassium leaks out.
  2. Acidosis drives an extracellular shift: H⁺ moves into cells to be buffered, and K⁺ moves out to preserve electroneutrality. More potassium leaves the cell.
  3. Hyperosmolality (from hyperglycaemia) drags water out of cells, and K⁺ follows the water by solvent drag. Yet more leaves the cell.
  4. The kidney, faced with an osmotic diuresis from glycosuria, then excretes vast amounts of the potassium now sitting in the extracellular space and urine. This is where the true, irreversible loss happens — potassium is poured down the drain.

So on arrival the serum K⁺ is often high (the cell is dumping potassium into the blood faster than the kidney can clear it), while the total-body store is being catastrophically emptied. The high number is a snapshot of a leaking bucket, not a full one.

In DKA the serum potassium runs high while total-body potassium runs empty. Treat the store, not the snapshot.
💡 The reversal at the moment of treatment

The instant you give insulin and correct the acidosis, every one of those shift mechanisms reverses. Insulin reactivates the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, correction of acidosis pulls K⁺ back into cells, and rehydration dilutes the serum. Potassium pours back into the cells — but there is far less of it than the serum number suggested, because the kidney already excreted the rest. The serum potassium therefore falls fast and hard within the first few hours of insulin, and this treatment-induced hypokalaemia — not the presenting acidosis — is the commonest preventable cause of death in DKA.

2 · ⚖️ THE RULE — potassium before and during insulin

The JBDS-IP management of DKA builds the whole potassium strategy around one non-negotiable sequence:

Check potassium before you start insulin. If K⁺ is below 3.5 mmol/L, do NOT start insulin until it is replaced. Add potassium to the fluids for everyone else, and monitor the heart.
  • Check K⁺ early and often — on the presenting venous blood gas (which gives potassium in minutes), then hourly-to-2-hourly on the VBG through the first several hours, and formally on lab U&E at baseline, 2 h, and then per protocol.
  • Do not start the fixed-rate insulin if K⁺ < 3.5 mmol/L. Insulin will drop it further and precipitate arrhythmia and respiratory-muscle failure. Rehydrate and replace potassium first, then start insulin once K⁺ is ≥ 3.5.
  • Add potassium chloride to the fluids for everyone whose K⁺ is under 5.5 mmol/L, according to the sliding table below.
  • Continuous cardiac monitoring for any patient with an abnormal potassium at presentation or receiving potassium replacement.

3 · 📊 The JBDS potassium sliding table — master this

This is the table to have burned into memory. Potassium is added to each litre of the intravenous fluid (usually 0.9% sodium chloride), and the rate of potassium delivery is governed by how much fluid is running:

Serum K⁺ (mmol/L)Potassium replacement (per litre of fluid)Action
> 5.5NoneDo not add potassium. Recheck in 1–2 h — it will fall.
3.5 – 5.540 mmol/L KCl (ready-mixed bag)The default for the great majority of DKA patients once insulin is running.
< 3.5Senior review — more than 40 mmol/L neededDo NOT start (or pause) insulin; give potassium via a monitored setting, often needing HDU/ICU and central access.
⚠️ The peripheral potassium ceiling

Potassium replacement above 40 mmol/L via a peripheral line is painful, causes phlebitis, and is generally unsafe. A patient who needs more than that — the K⁺ < 3.5 group — needs a high-dependency or ICU environment, continuous cardiac monitoring, ideally central venous access, and a senior decision. The maximum recommended peripheral rate is commonly cited as 10 mmol/hour; faster potassium delivery (up to 20 mmol/h) demands central access and continuous ECG. Never bolus concentrated potassium — undiluted KCl push is lethal.

💡 Why 40 mmol/L for almost everyone

Because the store is empty even when the number looks fine, most DKA patients whose K⁺ lands in the wide 3.5–5.5 band get 40 mmol/L in every litre from the moment insulin starts. You are not correcting a low number — you are pre-empting the fall that insulin is about to cause. Waiting for the potassium to drop before you act means you are always chasing it downhill.

4 · 🫀 Reading the potassium on the ECG

The monitor is your continuous potassium assay between blood gases. Learn both directions:

StateECG changesProgression if untreated
Hyperkalaemia (presenting)Tall, peaked, tented T waves; then flattened P, wide QRSSine wave → VF/asystole
Hypokalaemia (treatment-induced)Flattened/inverted T waves, U waves, ST depression, long QUVentricular ectopy → torsades/VT → arrest

In DKA the clinically dangerous drift is nearly always toward the second row — the treatment-induced hypokalaemia that appears once insulin has been running a few hours. The appearance of U waves on the monitor is a call to check a gas now and reassess the replacement rate.

5 · 🦴 Phosphate — the electrolyte you usually leave alone

Phosphate is depleted in DKA by the same osmotic-diuresis mechanism as potassium, and serum phosphate — like potassium — often looks normal or high on arrival before falling sharply with insulin. Yet routine phosphate replacement is NOT recommended. Multiple randomised trials have shown no benefit in clinical outcome, duration of DKA, or survival from routinely replacing phosphate, and over-aggressive replacement risks hypocalcaemia and hypomagnesaemia.

  • Replace only when phosphate is very low (typically < 0.3 mmol/L) and there is a clinical consequence — respiratory muscle weakness, cardiac dysfunction, or evidence of tissue hypoxia (phosphate is needed for 2,3-DPG and ATP).
  • When you do replace, do it cautiously and monitor calcium and magnesium, because phosphate infusion binds calcium.
Phosphate is depleted in DKA but replacing it routinely helps no one — reserve it for the very low, symptomatic patient.

6 · 🧲 Magnesium — the quiet co-factor

Hypomagnesaemia frequently accompanies DKA and is easy to forget. Its importance is largely permissive: you cannot correct hypokalaemia in the face of untreated hypomagnesaemia, because magnesium is required for the renal tubule to retain potassium and for the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase to function. A stubborn, refractory hypokalaemia that will not come up despite generous replacement is very often a magnesium problem in disguise. Magnesium deficiency also prolongs the QT and predisposes to torsades. Check magnesium in any DKA patient with refractory hypokalaemia or arrhythmia, and replace it (e.g. IV magnesium sulphate) alongside the potassium.

💡 The refractory-K rule

Potassium that will not rise despite adequate replacement = check and replace the magnesium. You cannot hold water in a bucket with a hole in it, and low magnesium is the hole.

7 · 🧪 The bicarbonate controversy — why we don't give it

It is tempting: the pH is 6.9, the patient looks dreadful, and there is a bottle of sodium bicarbonate on the resus trolley. Resist it. Bicarbonate is not recommended in the routine treatment of DKA. The acidosis of DKA is driven by ketoacid production, and it resolves as insulin and fluids switch off ketogenesis and the liver metabolises the ketoanions back to bicarbonate. Giving exogenous bicarbonate does not speed recovery — and it does real harm.

The harms of bicarbonate in DKA

HarmMechanism
Paradoxical CNS acidosisBicarbonate + H⁺ → CO₂, which crosses the blood–brain barrier freely and lowers CSF pH even as arterial pH rises. The brain gets more acidotic.
Worsened hypokalaemiaRapid correction of acidosis drives K⁺ into cells, deepening the very hypokalaemia that is the main killer.
Delayed ketone clearanceAlkali therapy has been shown to slow the fall in ketonaemia and lactate and prolong the metabolic recovery.
Left-shifted oxygen curveAbrupt alkalinisation impairs tissue oxygen offloading, and the sodium load can precipitate fluid overload and cerebral oedema (especially in children).

The only circumstance in which bicarbonate is even considered is extreme, life-threatening acidaemia (arterial pH < 6.9) in a haemodynamically unstable patient, and even then only in cautious, small doses in a critical-care setting after senior/ICU discussion — and the 2024 ADA/EASD consensus on hyperglycaemic crises reinforces that even at these extremes the evidence of benefit is absent and the practice is a pragmatic last resort, not a treatment.

DKA acidosis is cured by insulin, fluid and time — not by bicarbonate. The only debate is pH < 6.9, and even there the honest answer is "probably still no."

8 · 🧮 The master electrolyte-replacement table

ElectrolyteDirection in DKAAction
PotassiumTotal-body depleted; serum high then falls fast on insulinCheck before insulin; hold insulin if <3.5; add 40 mmol/L to fluids if 3.5–5.5; none if >5.5; senior/HDU if <3.5
PhosphateDepleted; falls with insulinDo NOT replace routinely; only if <0.3 and symptomatic (weakness, cardiac, respiratory)
MagnesiumOften lowReplace if refractory hypokalaemia, arrhythmia or long QT
BicarbonateLow (consumed by ketoacids)Do NOT give. Consider only if pH <6.9 + unstable, in ICU, senior-led
SodiumCorrected sodium often high; measured low from pseudohyponatraemiaGuides fluid choice; watch for rise as glucose falls

9 · 💀 M&M — insulin before potassium

⚠️ Morbidity & Mortality: "the gas was normal, so I didn't wait"

A 19-year-old presented in her first DKA: pH 7.06, glucose 28, and a presenting potassium of 3.3 mmol/L, flagged on the venous gas but not read by the team, who were focused on the glucose. Fixed-rate insulin was started immediately without potassium in the first bag. Within two hours she complained of leg weakness and palpitations; the repeat gas showed K⁺ 2.4 mmol/L with U waves and frequent ventricular ectopics on the monitor — which then degenerated into torsades and a VF arrest. She was resuscitated after prolonged CPR and emergency potassium, but suffered a hypoxic brain injury. The root cause was singular and avoidable: insulin was started before the potassium was addressed. The presenting K⁺ was already below 3.5 — insulin should have been held, potassium replaced in a monitored setting, and insulin started only once K⁺ was ≥ 3.5. The acidosis was never what threatened her life. The potassium was.

10 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Total-body potassium is depleted in every DKA patient (3–5 mmol/kg), even when the serum number is high — the number lies.
  2. Insulin drives potassium into cells, so serum K⁺ falls fast and hard once treatment starts; treatment-induced hypokalaemia is the commonest preventable cause of death in DKA.
  3. Check potassium before and early — the presenting VBG gives it in minutes; then hourly-to-2-hourly.
  4. If K⁺ < 3.5, do NOT start insulin until potassium is replaced in a monitored setting.
  5. The sliding table: >5.5 none · 3.5–5.5 add 40 mmol/L · <3.5 senior help + more, HDU/ICU.
  6. Continuous cardiac monitoring for any abnormal potassium or active replacement; watch for U waves.
  7. Do not replace phosphate routinely — only if very low and symptomatic — and watch calcium/magnesium if you do.
  8. Refractory hypokalaemia = check the magnesium.
  9. Do not give bicarbonate — it causes paradoxical CNS acidosis, worsens hypokalaemia and delays ketone clearance; consider only at pH < 6.9 in an unstable patient, ICU-led.

moderatorQs.q: The presenting potassium in a DKA patient is 5.9 mmol/L. Does this reassure you about their potassium status, and what will you add to the first bag of fluid?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: No — a high presenting potassium is falsely reassuring. Despite a serum K⁺ of 5.9, this patient is total-body potassium depleted (typically 3–5 mmol/kg) because acidosis, insulin deficiency and hyperosmolality have shifted potassium out of cells and the osmotic diuresis has then excreted it. The high number reflects a leaking store, not a full one. Because the value is above 5.5, you add no potassium to the first bag — but you must recheck within 1–2 hours, because insulin will drive it down rapidly, and as soon as it falls into the 3.5–5.5 band you switch to 40 mmol/L KCl per litre. The danger in this patient is not the presenting hyperkalaemia; it is the treatment-induced hypokalaemia coming a few hours later.

moderatorQs.q: A registrar wants to give 100 mL of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate to a DKA patient with a pH of 6.95 to 'buy time'. What is your answer and why?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The answer is no, other than in the most extreme, ICU-supervised circumstances. DKA acidosis is caused by ketoacid production and is corrected by insulin, fluid and time as ketogenesis switches off and ketoanions are metabolised back to bicarbonate. Exogenous bicarbonate does not accelerate this and causes measurable harm: it generates CO₂ that crosses into the CSF and produces a paradoxical central acidosis, it drives potassium into cells and worsens the hypokalaemia that is the main killer, and it has been shown to delay clearance of ketones and lactate. Bicarbonate is only even considered at a pH below 6.9 in a haemodynamically unstable patient, in critical care, after senior discussion — and even then the evidence of benefit is absent. At a pH of 6.95 the correct treatment is to ensure the fluids and insulin are optimised and the potassium is being managed.

moderatorQs.q: You have replaced potassium generously for six hours but the serum K⁺ remains stuck at 3.0 mmol/L. What are you missing?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The most likely missing piece is magnesium. Hypomagnesaemia is common in DKA and is permissive for hypokalaemia: magnesium is required for the renal tubule to retain potassium and for the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase to function, so you cannot correct hypokalaemia while the magnesium is low — the potassium you give is simply lost in the urine. Refractory hypokalaemia should trigger an immediate magnesium level and empirical replacement with IV magnesium sulphate. You should also confirm the potassium is actually being delivered (check the infusion rate and that the bags contain KCl), ensure cardiac monitoring is in place, and — if K⁺ is this low — pause the insulin, escalate to a senior, and manage the patient in an HDU/ICU setting with the higher replacement rates that require central access.

audienceQs.q: How often should I actually be checking the potassium in a DKA patient, and can I trust the value from the blood gas?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Check it before you start insulin (the presenting venous blood gas gives you potassium within minutes, and yes — the VBG potassium is reliable enough to guide immediate management), then hourly to 2-hourly on the gas through the first several hours when the fall is steepest, with a formal laboratory U&E at baseline and around 2 hours and then per your local DKA protocol. The gas value is what you act on in real time; the lab value is your cross-check. Any patient with an abnormal potassium or on active replacement should also be on continuous cardiac monitoring, so you have a live readout between blood draws — flattened T waves and U waves mean check a gas now.

audienceQs.q: What are the safe limits for how much and how fast potassium can be given, and when does the patient need to leave the ward?
audienceQs.answerHTML: On a general ward with peripheral access the safe ceiling is 40 mmol/L concentration and a rate of about 10 mmol/hour, using ready-mixed bags — never add concentrated potassium to a bag by hand and never give an IV bolus/push of potassium, which is lethal. Any patient who needs more than 40 mmol/L or faster than 10 mmol/h — essentially the K⁺ < 3.5 group — needs an HDU or ICU environment, continuous ECG monitoring and usually central venous access, plus a senior decision. That is also the group in whom insulin should be held until the potassium is ≥ 3.5, so flag it immediately if you see fixed-rate insulin prescribed alongside a potassium under 3.5.

audienceQs.q: Should I be routinely replacing phosphate in DKA? I see it depleted on the labs.
audienceQs.answerHTML: No — routine phosphate replacement is not recommended. Phosphate is genuinely depleted in DKA and, like potassium, falls further with insulin, but multiple randomised trials have shown that replacing it routinely does not improve outcomes, shorten the DKA, or reduce mortality — and over-replacement causes hypocalcaemia and hypomagnesaemia. Reserve replacement for the patient with a very low phosphate (roughly < 0.3 mmol/L) plus a clinical consequence — respiratory muscle weakness, cardiac dysfunction, or tissue hypoxia — since phosphate is needed for ATP and 2,3-DPG. If you do replace it, give it cautiously and monitor calcium and magnesium closely.
